$comment: The scope registry. This file must live where the repositories it governs cannot write to it —
a separate, restricted repository, alongside the trusted enforcement workflow. StandardsEnforcer
refuses a registry located inside the repository being assessed.
Entries are keyed by immutable platform identity, never by name. `acme/moneyball` can be renamed,
transferred, deleted and recreated by somebody else; a decision that follows a name follows
whoever holds the name today. `name` is present for humans and is never matched on.
Dispositions are filed under `standards`, keyed by the asking pack's own contract id, because the
unit of applicability is repository x standards pack. A repository may be in scope for one standard
and out of scope for another, each with its own reviewer, date, reason and basis. Silence about a
pack is a question, not an answer: no decision on file is review-required, and never inherits
another pack's decision.
`policyPath` names the policy file that governs this repository FOR THIS PACK, relative to the
repository root. Where it is present the enforcer refuses to default and refuses a --policy
naming anything else, so which policy governs is settled where the governed repository cannot
rewrite the answer. Comparison is by file rather than by spelling: case and separators are folded
on Windows, so a drive-letter difference is not reported as a governance conflict.
IT IS REQUIRED ONCE A REPOSITORY IS IN SCOPE FOR MORE THAN ONE PACK, and optional below that.
Every pack's init writes project-policy.yml and their schemas are mutually incompatible, so with
two or more dispositions in scope the default filename cannot say which document governs which
pack. A disposition that omits it there is review-required and nothing is evaluated -- the
registry is well-formed and a human under-specified it. With exactly one pack in scope the default
is unambiguous and requiring this would be ceremony.
acme/pricing-engine below is the multi-pack shape, and it carries the one consequence people get
wrong: the pack whose policy sits at the DEFAULT location must name it too. Being the incumbent is
not an exemption. Once a second pack is in scope, `project-policy.yml` is one candidate among
several rather than the obvious answer, and the requirement is on every in-scope disposition.
The pack ids in this file are opaque data -- each is a pack's own `standard.id`, read from the
adapter contract in its verified release. The enforcer holds no list of them and validates nothing
about them beyond presence: an id it has never seen simply has no disposition on file, which is
review-required. Governing a repository with a third or fourth pack is an edit to THIS file and to
nothing in scripts/ (ADR 0001).
`reviewedFootprint` is the evidence basis, and it NAMES THE SURFACE it was reviewed against. It is
what makes a decision able to go stale, and a decision that cannot go stale cannot be trusted to be
fresh. Obtain it with `node scripts/footprint.mjs <dir>`. A basis naming a surface the enforcer did
not observe on a run is undetermined — neither fresh nor stale — and goes back to a human. There is
one detector today; a pack with no detector is not a pack whose detector found nothing.
An out-of-scope entry needs exactly the same quality of record as an in-scope one. An exclusion
is a governance decision, not an absence of evidence.

github:4096227.name: acme/pricing-engine
$comment: IN SCOPE FOR TWO PACKS, so every in-scope disposition here names its own policyPath -- the
engineering one included, even though its policy is the file the enforcer would have defaulted
to. That is the point: with a second pack in scope, the default location stops identifying a
document. Omit it on either disposition and the answer is review-required, not a verdict.
Both bases name `training-evidence` because that is the one surface the enforcer computes
today, not because both packs are about training. A basis naming a surface no detector
produces is undetermined -- neither fresh nor stale -- and goes back to a human.
